question: A woman who is 15 days post-partum and exclusively breastfeeding presents after unprotected sexual intercourse last night. She asks if she needs emergency contraception. Per FSRH guidance on the lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM), what should she be advised?

options.A: She needs emergency contraception immediately — breastfeeding provides no protection
options.B: The lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM) is >98% effective if ALL three criteria are met: baby <6 months old, fully breastfeeding (no formula supplementation, no breast pump substitution), and no periods have returned. She meets all three criteria at 15 days post-partum — emergency contraception is not required
options.C: She should take the copper IUD only — no oral emergency contraception is effective during breastfeeding
options.D: LAM only works after 6 weeks post-partum
options.E: She must use contraception immediately — LAM is not a recognised method

explanation.correct: Per FSRH guidance on lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM): LAM is a recognised, evidence-based contraceptive method with >98% effectiveness when all three criteria are met simultaneously: (1) Baby <6 months old — beyond 6 months, ovulation becomes increasingly likely; (2) Fully/exclusively breastfeeding — at least 4-hourly feeds during the day and 6-hourly at night; no formula supplementation; (3) No menstrual periods have returned. This patient: 15 days post-partum (✓), exclusively breastfeeding (✓), no periods (✓ — periods don't typically return for weeks-months post-partum in breastfeeding women). All three criteria met — LAM is effective and emergency contraception is not required. She should be counselled about when to add another method (if any criterion changes).
explanation.A: Incorrect — LAM is a recognised >98% effective method when all three criteria are met — this patient meets all three.
explanation.B: CORRECT — All three LAM criteria met (baby <6 months, fully breastfeeding, no periods) — no emergency contraception needed per FSRH.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Oral emergency contraception (levonorgestrel, ulipristal) can be used while breastfeeding with appropriate precautions if needed.
explanation.D: Incorrect — LAM begins immediately post-partum and is effective from day 1 if all criteria are met.
explanation.E: Incorrect — LAM is a WHO and FSRH-recognised method with >98% effectiveness when criteria are met.

reference: FSRH — Lactational amenorrhoea method. WHO — Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use. https://www.fsrh.org/standards-and-guidance/

question: A 39-year-old woman has been on the levonorgestrel IUS (Mirena 52mg) for contraception for 2 years. She now presents with hot flushes, night sweats and mood changes. Her GP confirms she is perimenopausal (FSH >30, confirmed on two occasions). Per NICE NG23 and FSRH guidance, what is the appropriate management?

options.A: Stop the Mirena and start a combined HRT patch
options.B: Add oestrogen-only HRT (transdermal oestradiol patch or gel) — the Mirena IUS provides the progestogen component needed for endometrial protection; adding oestrogen-only HRT completes the combined preparation required for menopausal symptoms without the need to add separate progestogen
options.C: Prescribe progestogen-only HRT only — oestrogen is not needed
options.D: No HRT is needed — Mirena alone treats menopausal symptoms
options.E: Remove Mirena and start COCP for menopausal symptoms

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG23 (Menopause: diagnosis and management) and FSRH guidance: the levonorgestrel IUS (Mirena) is licensed to provide the progestogen component of combined HRT in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women with a uterus. By adding oestrogen-only HRT (transdermal oestradiol — patch, gel, spray), the Mirena provides the endometrial protection (preventing oestrogen-stimulated endometrial hyperplasia/cancer), completing the HRT regimen. This approach: (1) Provides effective contraception (Mirena is also highly effective contraceptive); (2) Provides endometrial protection; (3) The oestrogen component treats vasomotor symptoms. FSRH guidance supports this as an established HRT regimen. Advantages: combined HRT without extra pill burden. A woman with a uterus needs progestogen WITH oestrogen HRT to prevent endometrial cancer.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Stopping the Mirena and starting combined HRT is not necessary — the Mirena already provides the progestogen component.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Mirena provides progestogen protection; add oestrogen-only HRT for vasomotor symptoms per NICE NG23/FSRH.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Progestogen-only treatment does not adequately treat menopausal vasomotor symptoms — oestrogen is the key component.
explanation.D: Incorrect — The Mirena is a progestogen-only device and does not contain oestrogen to treat vasomotor symptoms.
explanation.E: Incorrect — COCP contains synthetic oestrogen/progestogen — not appropriate for menopausal HRT and removes the Mirena benefit.

reference: NICE NG23 — Menopause. FSRH — Hormonal contraception and HRT. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng23

question: A 26-year-old woman presents with weight gain, acne, hirsutism, irregular periods (every 45-90 days) and difficulty conceiving for 18 months. Ultrasound shows bilateral polycystic ovaries and testosterone is mildly elevated. Per NICE CG156, what is the diagnosis and initial management?

options.A: Hypothyroidism — check TFTs and start levothyroxine
options.B: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) — management: lifestyle modifications (weight loss is the most effective intervention for improving menstrual regularity, fertility and hyperandrogenism); for menstrual irregularity: COCP or cyclical progestogen; for hirsutism: COCP (especially Dianette — co-cyprindiol); for fertility: ovulation induction with clomifene or letrozole; metformin for insulin resistance
options.E: Primary ovarian insufficiency — FSH levels and HRT

explanation.correct: PCOS (Rotterdam criteria: 2 of 3): oligo/anovulation (irregular periods), hyperandrogenism (clinical/biochemical), polycystic ovaries on USS. Per NICE CG156 (Fertility: assessment and treatment): lifestyle modifications — weight loss (even 5-10% of body weight in overweight women significantly improves menstrual regularity, ovulation and fertility); first-line pharmacological: COCP (for menstrual regulation and hirsutism — co-cyprindiol/Dianette for hirsutism), metformin (improves insulin sensitivity, menstrual regularity, ovulation induction adjunct); for fertility: letrozole (first-line in UK per updated guidance, superior to clomifene) or clomifene for ovulation induction. Referral to reproductive medicine if not conceiving after 6 cycles of ovulation induction. Exclude other causes: thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, CAH (17-OH progesterone), Cushing's.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Hypothyroidism can cause irregular periods but not hirsutism or polycystic ovaries — TFTs should be checked but PCOS is the primary diagnosis.
explanation.B: CORRECT — PCOS: weight loss + COCP for menstrual regulation/hirsutism + letrozole/clomifene for fertility per NICE CG156.
explanation.C: Incorrect — CAH is important to exclude (17-OHP) in hirsute women but the full clinical picture (polycystic ovaries on USS + the classic PCOS features) strongly suggests PCOS.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Prolactinoma causes hyperprolactinaemia with galactorrhoea and irregular periods without the full PCOS picture.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Primary ovarian insufficiency causes elevated FSH with low oestrogen and hot flushes in younger women — different from PCOS.

reference: NICE CG156 — Fertility: assessment and treatment. NICE CKS — PCOS. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg156

question: A 28-year-old woman presents for her 8-week antenatal booking appointment. Her GP notes she is on lisinopril for hypertension. Her BP today is 142/88 mmHg. Per NICE NG133 (Hypertension in pregnancy), what must be done?

options.A: Continue lisinopril — ACE inhibitors are safe in early pregnancy
options.B: Stop lisinopril immediately — ACE inhibitors and ARBs are teratogenic (renal dysplasia, oligohydramnios, IUGR, neonatal renal failure in 2nd/3rd trimester); switch to labetalol (first-line in UK), methyldopa, or nifedipine modified release; target BP <135/85 mmHg in pregnancy
options.C: Stop lisinopril and start no alternative — hypertension does not need treating in early pregnancy
options.D: Reduce lisinopril dose by half — safe in first trimester
options.E: Refer to cardiology before making any medication changes

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG133 (Hypertension in pregnancy), ACE inhibitors (lisinopril, ramipril, enalapril) and ARBs (losartan, valsartan) are CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy: first trimester — associated with cardiac malformations (some evidence); second and third trimester — definitive teratogenic effects: oligohydramnios (reduced amniotic fluid), renal tubular dysplasia, fetal anuria, IUGR, pulmonary hypoplasia, neonatal renal failure. Should be stopped as soon as pregnancy is confirmed. Safe antihypertensives in pregnancy per NICE NG133: labetalol (beta-blocker — first-line), nifedipine MR (dihydropyridine CCB — second-line), methyldopa (alpha-agonist — alternative). Target BP: <135/85 mmHg for pre-existing hypertension in pregnancy. Aspirin 75-150mg from 12 weeks if high risk of pre-eclampsia.
explanation.A: Incorrect — ACE inhibitors are teratogenic — they must be stopped immediately when pregnancy is confirmed.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Stop lisinopril immediately + switch to labetalol (first-line) per NICE NG133. ACE inhibitors/ARBs are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Chronic hypertension requires treatment in pregnancy — untreated hypertension increases risk of pre-eclampsia, abruption and stroke.
explanation.D: Incorrect — No dose of lisinopril is safe in pregnancy — complete cessation and switch is required.
explanation.E: Incorrect — This is a primary care emergency requiring immediate medication change — cardiology referral would unnecessarily delay safe treatment.

reference: NICE NG133 — Hypertension in pregnancy. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng133

question: A 62-year-old post-menopausal woman on tamoxifen for breast cancer develops light vaginal spotting. She has no other symptoms. Per NICE CG81 and RCOG guidance, what must be done immediately?

options.A: Reassure — post-menopausal bleeding on tamoxifen is an expected side effect
options.B: Urgent transvaginal USS to measure endometrial thickness — tamoxifen stimulates the endometrium (partial oestrogen agonist effect on uterus) and significantly increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial carcinoma; endometrial thickness >4mm in post-menopausal women warrants hysteroscopy and biopsy
options.C: Start combined HRT — oestrogen thins the endometrium
options.D: Stop tamoxifen immediately — the only management
options.E: Prescribe norethisterone to stop the bleeding

explanation.correct: Per NICE CG81 (Heavy menstrual bleeding) and RCOG guidance, any post-menopausal bleeding (PMB) must be investigated to exclude endometrial carcinoma. Tamoxifen: selective oestrogen receptor modulator (SERM) — anti-oestrogenic in breast tissue (therapeutic for breast cancer) but pro-oestrogenic in the uterus. Long-term tamoxifen significantly increases endometrial cancer risk (2.5-7.5× baseline). Post-menopausal bleeding on tamoxifen = red flag requiring: urgent (2WW per NICE NG12) transvaginal USS measuring endometrial thickness; if >4mm: hysteroscopy + endometrial biopsy; if <4mm but symptoms persist: biopsy still recommended given the high-risk context (tamoxifen use). NICE NG12: post-menopausal bleeding is a 2WW referral criterion regardless of cause.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Post-menopausal bleeding is NEVER normal and always requires investigation to exclude endometrial malignancy.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Urgent transvaginal USS + endometrial biopsy if thickness >4mm for PMB on tamoxifen per NICE CG81/NG12.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Starting HRT in a patient on tamoxifen for breast cancer would be clinically hazardous and contraindicated.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Stopping tamoxifen without oncology input would compromise breast cancer treatment — the bleeding must be investigated.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Prescribing norethisterone to stop PMB without investigating the cause risks masking endometrial carcinoma.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer. NICE CG81 — Heavy menstrual bleeding. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 32-year-old woman presents with a 3-year history of severe dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, dyschezia (painful defaecation) and subfertility. Per NICE NG73, what is the definitive diagnostic procedure for endometriosis?

options.A: Transvaginal ultrasound — sufficient to diagnose endometriosis
options.B: Laparoscopy with biopsy — the gold standard for definitive diagnosis of endometriosis; allows direct visualisation of endometriotic lesions, ovarian endometriomas, adhesions and deep infiltrating disease; histological confirmation of endometrial glands/stroma confirms the diagnosis
options.C: CA-125 serum level — elevated in endometriosis and diagnostic
options.E: Diagnostic criteria are entirely clinical — no investigation needed

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG73 (Endometriosis: diagnosis and management), laparoscopy is the definitive diagnostic investigation for endometriosis. Clinical features (dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia, chronic pelvic pain, subfertility) raise suspicion but are insufficient alone for diagnosis. TVUSS: useful for detecting ovarian endometriomas (chocolate cysts) and deep infiltrating endometriosis but not sensitive/specific for peritoneal disease or superficial lesions. MRI: superior to USS for deep infiltrating endometriosis (bowel, bladder, uterosacral ligaments) but still not definitive. CA-125: elevated in endometriosis and malignancy — low sensitivity and specificity; not diagnostic. Laparoscopy: allows direct visualisation + biopsy for histological confirmation; also therapeutic (excision/ablation of deposits). Per NICE NG73: do not exclude endometriosis based on normal USS or CA-125 — laparoscopy is required for definitive diagnosis.
explanation.A: Incorrect — TVUSS misses peritoneal and superficial endometriosis — it cannot definitively diagnose or exclude endometriosis.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Laparoscopy with biopsy is the gold standard for definitive endometriosis diagnosis per NICE NG73.
explanation.C: Incorrect — CA-125 has poor sensitivity and specificity for endometriosis — it is not diagnostic.
explanation.D: Incorrect — MRI is useful for staging deep disease but is not sufficient as the definitive diagnostic test.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Clinical diagnosis alone is insufficient — histological confirmation via laparoscopy is required per NICE NG73.

reference: NICE NG73 — Endometriosis: diagnosis and management. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng73
